definition: A binary heap is a complete binary tree which satisfies the heap ordering property.
details: A binary heap is a complete binary tree which satisfies the heap ordering property. It can be seen as a binary tree with two additional constraints: the shape property and the heap property, often used in priority queues.

explainer.lead: A binary heap keeps a collection arranged so that the smallest or largest item is always at the top, without keeping the whole collection sorted. That makes it a practical foundation for priority queues and heapsort, with insertion and top-item removal taking O(log n) time.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a tournament chart where every player must be at least as strong as the two players below them. The strongest player is always on top, and a new player takes the next open spot, swapping upward until the rule holds. You can find the champion immediately, but finding one particular player may still mean checking everyone.
tiers.practitioner: Store the heap implicitly in an array, using positions rather than child pointers: insert at the end and sift up, or replace the root with the last element and sift down for extraction. Both operations take O(log n) worst-case time, while arbitrary search is O(n). Python provides heappushpop and heapreplace to combine insertion and extraction with one down-heap operation; remember that a heap is not a sorted array.
tiers.paperLevel: A binary heap is a complete binary tree, with the last level filled left to right, whose keys satisfy a total order: each parent key is ≥ its children's keys in a max-heap or ≤ them in a min-heap. J. W. J. Williams introduced it in 1964 as a data structure for implementing heapsort. Insertion and root extraction are O(log n), but arbitrary-element search is O(n).

explainer.example: In a max-heap whose root is 11 and whose child is 8, inserting 15 first places it in the leftmost open slot below 8. Since 15 > 8, swap them; since 15 > 11, swap again. The final root is 15, and no further swaps are needed.

usedIn.name: Priority queues
usedIn.detail: Supports logarithmic-time insertion and removal of the minimum or maximum element.

usedIn.name: Heapsort
usedIn.detail: Uses an array-backed binary heap as an implicit data structure, allowing in-place sorting.

usedIn.name: Python heap operations
usedIn.detail: heappushpop and heapreplace combine insertion and extraction to avoid separate up-heap and down-heap passes.

explainer.intuition: A heap maintains just enough order to make the extreme item cheap to reach: every parent outranks its children, but the rest of the collection need not be sorted. Its complete, left-filled shape keeps the tree shallow and lets array positions encode parent-child relationships.
howItWorks: Choose a min-heap to keep the smallest key at the root, or a max-heap to keep the largest key there.
Keep every level full except possibly the last, filling that level from left to right.
Insert at the leftmost open slot, then swap upward with parents until the heap ordering holds.
Extract the root by moving the last element into its place, then swapping downward with the appropriate child until ordering is restored.
explainer.whyItMatters: Binary heaps provide the two essential priority-queue operations efficiently while remaining compact enough to store in an array. This combination also makes them central to the in-place heapsort algorithm.
misconceptions: A heap is not fully sorted: finding an arbitrary element takes O(n) time.
Shape and ordering are separate constraints: updates first preserve the complete shape, then restore parent-child ordering.
A heap does not need explicit tree pointers: an array's relative positions can represent children and parents.
